title: Getting to the Top of Mind: How Reminders Increase Saving
abstract: We provide evidence from field experiments with three different banks that reminder messages increase commitment attainment for clients who recently opened commitment savings accounts. Messages that mention both savings goals and financial incentives are particularly effective, whereas other content variations such as gain versus loss framing do not have significantly different effects. Nor do we find evidence that receiving additional late reminders has an additive effect. These empirical results do not map neatly into existing models, so we provide a simple model where limited attention to exceptional expenses can generate undersaving that is in turn mitigated by reminders. Data, as supplemental material, are available at http://dx.doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2015.2296 . This paper was accepted by Teck-Hua Ho, behavioral economics.

claims.text: Monthly reminder messages increased total savings balances by 6% across pooled field experiment samples.
Monthly reminders increased the likelihood of clients reaching their savings goal by 3.1 percentage points.
Reminders that mentioned a specific expenditure goal increased savings balances by approximately 16% relative to no reminders.
Reminders that did not mention a specific expenditure goal did not have a statistically significant effect on savings amounts in Peru.
Visual treatments depicting the client's goal, such as photos or puzzle pieces, had no statistically significant impact on savings.
Reminders produced a larger increase in savings balances for individuals identified ex-ante as time-inconsistent.
Varying reminder framing between gain and loss language did not generate statistically significant differences in savings outcomes.
Sending late reminders to clients who missed deposit dates had no statistically significant additive effect on savings.
Reminders in Bolivia significantly increased savings only when they mentioned financial incentives alongside the savings goal.
Limited attention to future lumpy expenditures theoretically leads to undersaving and reduced intertemporal consumption smoothing.

limitations.text: The theoretical model does not account for consumer awareness of limited attention or market competition for limited attention.
The experimental data do not cover household full balance sheets, making it impossible to determine if reminders shifted total savings or crowded out savings elsewhere.
The sample consists solely of individuals who opened a savings account voluntarily, leaving open whether attention treatments affect non-savers.
Direct mail reminders incurred delivery costs of nearly one dollar per letter in Peru, rendering them not cost-effective for small-balance accounts.
Standard intertemporal choice models cannot reconcile observed borrowing and saving patterns without positing implausibly high short-term discount rates.

future_work.text: Investigate whether present-biased attention and present-biased preferences coexist, correlate, or dominate across different decision domains.
Measure comprehensive balance sheets to test whether reminders crowd out alternative savings instruments or induce borrowing.
Study whether firms compete for consumer attention and whether lenders exploit inattention by providing on-demand financing tied to specific expenditures.
Evaluate the dynamics of reminder frequency and whether repeated reminders foster habit formation or cause consumers to tune out.

methodologies.name: Multi-site Randomized Controlled Trial of Savings Reminders
methodologies.description: Randomized evaluation testing text message and mail reminders with varied timing, framing, and content across three partner banks in Bolivia, Peru, and the Philippines.
datasets: First Valley Bank Gihandom savings data (Philippines)
Caja de Ica Plan Ahorro savings data (Peru)
conditions: Late reminder conditional on missed deposit
Specific expenditure goal mention vs. standard boilerplate reminder
Financial incentive mention vs. non-incentive reminder
